claim: iOS Assistive Access is a distinct iOS mode designed for cognitive disabilities: bigger onscreen items, more focused features, easier navigation — Apple's stated design principles.
verbatim_quote: Assistive Access is a distinctive iOS experience that makes it easier for people with cognitive disabilities to use iPhone independently. ... onscreen items are bigger, features are more focused, and it's easier to navigate and understand what actions are possible.

claim: Assistive Access offers two home-screen layouts chosen at setup: Grid (bigger items, icon/image-emphasized) and Rows (readable list).
verbatim_quote: Rows: Onscreen items are arranged in an easily readable list. Grid: Onscreen items are bigger and arranged in a grid that emphasizes images and icons.
notes: Two layout archetypes: icon-grid vs list — user/caretaker picks per preference for visuals vs text.

claim: Assistive Access uses a 'trusted supporter' model: a family member or caregiver performs setup and personalization, including account/passcode access, entirely outside the mode.
verbatim_quote: Assistive Access may be easiest to set up with the assistance of a trusted supporter—a family member or caregiver who knows the person who will be using iPhone and can help them choose the apps and features best suited to their needs.

claim: Assistive Access is gated by its own passcode (separate from device passcode) used to enter, exit, and change settings; exit is triple-click side/Home button + passcode. A recovery Apple Account can be set so a caretaker can reset it remotely.
verbatim_quote: Set an Assistive Access passcode, which is used to enter or exit Assistive Access and change Assistive Access settings. ... To exit Assistive Access at any time, triple-click the side button (on an iPhone with Face ID) or the Home button (on other iPhone models), tap Exit Assistive Access, then enter the Assistive Access passcode.
notes: Caretaker-lock pattern: user inside mode cannot escape or reconfigure without passcode.

claim: In Assistive Access, Phone and FaceTime are merged into a single 'Calls' app; the supporter whitelists who can call/be called (anyone, all contacts, or favorites only) and favorites appear on the app's first screen.
verbatim_quote: the Phone and FaceTime apps are combined into a single Calls app ... Favorite contacts are shown on the first screen when the Calls app is opened in Assistive Access.
notes: Patterns: merge overlapping apps into one task-named app; favorites-first screen; inbound+outbound contact whitelisting.

claim: Assistive Access requires confirmation for committal actions: ending a call and declining a call each require tapping the button twice to confirm; a persistent Back button exists on every screen.
verbatim_quote: To hang up, tap End Call, then tap End Call again to confirm. ... On any screen in Assistive Access, the person using Assistive Access can always tap Back to return to the previous screen.

claim: Assistive Access suppresses runtime permission pop-ups — the supporter pre-sets app permissions during setup; Settings app, notifications, status icons (network, Bluetooth, location, Airplane Mode) are removed entirely inside the mode.
verbatim_quote: To minimize pop-ups while using iPhone, apps won't ask for permission to access information such as location, photos, and contacts. ... there is no Settings app or notifications in Assistive Access ... Certain app privacy information, status icons, and symbols aren't available in Assistive Access, including those that indicate network availability, Airplane Mode, Focus, or Bluetooth
notes: Removes-vs-keeps list: no pop-ups, no Settings, no notifications, no status bar indicators.

claim: Assistive Access Messages supports an emoji-only keyboard and video-selfie messages as visual alternatives to text; messages can be read aloud via Tap to Hear.
verbatim_quote: messages can be sent with an emoji-only keyboard or as a video selfie
notes: Visual-first communication alternatives; Tap-to-hear detail from Messages page (see open angles).

claim: Third-party apps can be added to Assistive Access only in their original form — only Apple's optimized apps (Calls, Camera, Messages, Music, Photos, Magnifier, TV) get the simplified treatment; App Store is not accessible inside the mode.
verbatim_quote: You can add apps that have been optimized for Assistive Access, and most other iOS apps in their original design.
notes: App Store exclusion documented on the add/remove-apps page; simplification only works where Apple redesigned the app.

claim: Samsung Easy Mode is a display-level toggle (Settings > Display > Easy mode) that enlarges on-screen items, provides a high-contrast keyboard, and increases touch-and-hold delay to prevent accidental touches — all other apps/settings remain intact.
verbatim_quote: It will enlarge the on-screen items, provide a high contrast keyboard, and help prevent accidental touches when tapping. From Settings, tap Display, and then tap Easy mode.
notes: Contrast with Apple: same user, reversible switch, no separate environment or passcode.

claim: Samsung Easy Mode restructures the launcher into dedicated panels: left home screen holds a Magnifier widget, another panel is a Contacts page where favorite contacts can be pinned to the home screen for quick calling.
verbatim_quote: Swipe to the left your Home Screen ... Tap on Magnifier ... Swipe across the Home Screen to view your Contacts page ... Select Create Contact or Add existing contact
notes: Pattern: dedicate a home-screen page to favorite contacts (call-by-face) and another to a magnifier tool.

claim: Xiaomi Lite mode is a home-screen style option (Settings > Home screen > Home screen > Lite mode) intended to make the phone 'easier to view, understand and operate'; a persistent 'Lite mode is on' entry in Settings provides an always-visible exit path.
verbatim_quote: The Xiaomi smartphone supports the Lite mode, making the phone easier to view, understand and operate. ... To turn off this function, please go to [Settings] and tap on [Lite mode is on]. Then tap [Turn off Lite mode].
notes: Pattern: sticky discoverable exit affordance inside Settings while mode is active.

claim: Huawei EMUI Simple Mode enlarges home-screen icons and fonts, simplifies layout, and automatically maximizes volume — uniquely addressing hearing as well as vision; long-press icon editing is retained and exit is a one-tap 'Exit Simple mode' in Settings.
verbatim_quote: Simple mode adopts a more concise layout for easy navigation, enlarges icons and fonts for the home screen, and maximizes the volume. ... Touch and hold any icon to drag it to the desired location or uninstall it if it is not a mandatory app.
notes: Auto max volume = multi-sensory accommodation; keeps layout editable rather than locked.

claim: Stock Android offers no unified senior mode but granular accessibility levers: font size up to 200%, independent display-size slider, bold text, outline/high-contrast text, color correction (4 profiles + intensity), color inversion, remove animations, and extra dim — surfaced in Quick Settings and the first-boot setup wizard.
verbatim_quote: You can adjust font size up to 200%. ... You can also find accessibility settings in quick settings ... These settings can also be set up from the start in the setup wizard.
notes: A senior launcher on Android should pre-compose these levers rather than expecting users to find them.

claim: Pattern: caretaker-configured contact whitelists (favorites-first, restrict inbound/outbound) appear in Apple's model; Samsung/Xiaomi/Huawei modes instead pin contacts to home screens without restricting who can call.
verbatim_quote: Allow the person using Assistive Access to receive calls from anyone, from all contacts in the Contacts app, or from favorite contacts only
notes: Synthesis across Apple vs Android OEM modes; Android modes are cosmetic, Apple's is a gated environment.

claim: Pattern: Android OEM simple modes (Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei) are single-toggle, user-reversible display changes that keep all apps and settings reachable; only Apple's Assistive Access is a locked, passcode-gated environment with administration moved entirely outside the mode.
verbatim_quote: From Settings, tap Display, and then tap Easy mode. Tap the switch to turn it on.
notes: Two architectures: cosmetic launcher swap vs separate accessibility environment. BaldPhone-style products target the former or a launcher-app version of the latter.

claim: Pattern: accidental-touch mitigation via timing — Samsung Easy Mode lengthens the touch-and-hold recognition delay so icons aren't moved/triggered by unsteady taps.
verbatim_quote: help prevent accidental touches when tapping
notes: Configurable long-press delay detail also confirmed in Samsung DE/JP Easy Mode pages (not separately noted).

claim: Pattern: confirmation-everything vs prevention — Apple re-asks on every committal action inside the mode; Samsung prevents the accidental input up front via touch timing. Both address tremor/unsteady touch.
verbatim_quote: tap End Call, then tap End Call again to confirm
notes: Design trade-off: double-confirm adds friction; longer-press adds latency. Worth testing both.

claim: Pattern: keep emergency paths unconditional — emergency calling in Assistive Access works even when the phone is locked via hardware-button triple-click, independent of contact whitelists.
verbatim_quote: You can make an emergency call while Assistive Access is active, even if iPhone is locked.
notes: Any senior-mode design must never let simplification gating block emergency calls.

claim: Pattern: visual-over-text defaults — Apple's grid layout emphasizes images/icons, contacts are shown as photo+name, and emoji-keyboard/video messages replace typing; the alternative 'Rows' list exists for users who prefer text.
verbatim_quote: Assistive Access offers ways for people to navigate iPhone and communicate using visuals rather than text.
